# Machine-Learned Noise Models for Quantum Error Mitigation on NISQ Processors

## 1. Background and motivation

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors now offer between 50 and a few
hundred qubits, but they remain limited by decoherence, gate infidelity, readout error,
and crosstalk. Without full fault-tolerant error correction, which demands physical
qubit counts and gate fidelities still out of reach, the near-term path to useful
computation runs through error *mitigation* rather than error *correction*. Error
mitigation accepts that the hardware is noisy and instead post-processes results, or
adjusts circuits, so that expectation values approach their noise-free counterparts.

Two mitigation techniques dominate current practice. Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE)
runs a circuit at several artificially amplified noise levels and extrapolates the
measured expectation value back to the zero-noise limit. Probabilistic error
cancellation (PEC) represents the inverse of the noise channel as a quasi-probability
distribution over implementable operations, then samples from it so that the averaged
result is unbiased. Both methods share a single structural dependency: they need a model
of the device noise. ZNE needs to know how noise scales when it is amplified; PEC needs
an explicit characterisation of each noisy gate so that its inverse can be constructed.

The accuracy of mitigation is therefore bounded by the accuracy of the noise model.
Today most deployments use a simple noise model, typically a depolarising or Pauli
channel fitted to a handful of randomised-benchmarking numbers, or a sparse model
calibrated through gate-set tomography on one or two qubits. These models are cheap but
crude. They assume noise is local, Markovian, time-stationary, and independent across
qubits. Real devices violate every one of those assumptions. Crosstalk couples
spatially separated gates, control electronics drift over minutes to hours, and
non-Markovian memory effects appear in superconducting and trapped-ion platforms alike.
When the model is wrong, PEC produces biased estimates and ZNE extrapolates along the
wrong curve.

This proposal asks whether a machine-learned noise model, trained directly on device
measurements, can capture the spatial and temporal structure that hand-built models
miss, and whether feeding such a model into PEC and ZNE measurably improves mitigated
expectation values on real NISQ hardware. The central idea is not to replace the
physics but to let a flexible function approximator absorb the residual structure that
the physics-based model leaves on the table.

## 2. Hypothesis and research questions

**Primary hypothesis.** A noise model parameterised by a neural network and trained on
randomised-circuit measurements will predict device error channels more accurately than
a standard sparse Pauli-Lindblad baseline, and substituting it into PEC will reduce the
bias of mitigated expectation values on a 27-qubit superconducting processor by a factor
of at least two at fixed sampling cost, for circuits up to depth 40.

We decompose this into four research questions.

**RQ1.** Can a learned model predict held-out error rates (for gate combinations and
qubit subsets not seen during training) more accurately than the Pauli-Lindblad
baseline, measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence on a tomographically characterised
test set?

**RQ2.** Does the learned model recover known crosstalk and drift structure that the
baseline ignores, and can we attribute its predictions to physically interpretable terms
through an ablation of its input features?

**RQ3.** When the learned model is plugged into PEC and ZNE, does the bias of mitigated
expectation values fall, and by how much, relative to the same protocols using the
baseline model, at matched shot budgets?

**RQ4.** How does the advantage scale with circuit depth and qubit number, and at what
point does the sampling overhead of PEC erase the benefit?

Stating the hypothesis quantitatively, with a fixed sampling budget and a defined
circuit family, makes the project falsifiable. If the learned model fails to beat the
baseline on RQ1, the downstream questions become moot, and we report that cleanly.

## 3. Related work and positioning

Gate-set tomography gives an exhaustive characterisation of a small qubit register but
scales exponentially and cannot cover a full device. Randomised benchmarking and its
variants give scalable but coarse summaries, typically a single average error rate per
gate. Sparse Pauli-Lindblad models, which underpin recent large-scale PEC demonstrations,
strike a balance: they assume the generator of the noise channel is a sum of a tractable
number of Pauli terms whose rates are learned from cycle benchmarking. This is the
state-of-the-art baseline we target, and we deliberately do not strawman it.

Machine learning has been applied to quantum control, to readout-error classification,
and to learning syndrome decoders for error-corrected codes. Our contribution sits in a
less crowded space: learning the *generator* of a continuous noise channel for the
explicit purpose of inverting it inside a mitigation protocol. The closest prior work
treats the noise model as a black box that predicts corrected expectation values
directly, skipping the channel. We argue that learning the channel, rather than the
corrected output, keeps the method compatible with the unbiasedness guarantee of PEC and
yields an interpretable object that can be audited against physics. That interpretability
is a design choice with a cost, discussed in the risks section.

## 4. Methods

### 4.1 Hardware and platform

The primary platform is a 27-qubit fixed-frequency transmon device accessed through a
cloud provider, with calibration data exposed per job. We will also run a subset of
experiments on a trapped-ion device with all-to-all connectivity to test whether
conclusions transfer across hardware with different dominant noise mechanisms. Using two
physically distinct platforms guards against a result that is really a quirk of one
device.

### 4.2 Data collection

Training data comes from randomised circuits in the mirror-circuit family, where the
ideal output is known by construction, so any deviation is attributable to noise. For
each circuit we record the full measured bitstring distribution over many shots, along
with the device calibration metadata at execution time: per-qubit T1 and T2, single- and
two-qubit gate errors, readout assignment matrices, and timestamps. We will collect data
across several weeks to capture drift, and we will interleave circuits spatially to
sample crosstalk between many qubit pairs. Each record is therefore a (circuit,
calibration context, measured distribution) triple.

### 4.3 Model architecture

The learned model predicts the rates of a Pauli-Lindblad generator, but instead of one
fitted rate per term it outputs the rates as a function of context. The architecture is a
graph neural network whose nodes are qubits and whose edges follow the device coupling
map. Node and edge features include the calibration metadata, the gates scheduled in the
current layer, and the gates scheduled in neighbouring sites (to expose crosstalk). The
network outputs a vector of Pauli-Lindblad rates for the layer. By embedding the output
in the same Pauli-Lindblad form as the baseline, we keep the channel physically
well-formed (completely positive and trace preserving) and directly invertible for PEC.

This is a deliberate constraint. A fully unconstrained network could fit the training
distributions better but might output non-physical channels that PEC cannot invert. We
trade a little expressivity for a guarantee that the learned object is usable downstream.

### 4.4 Training objective

The model is trained to minimise the divergence between the distribution it predicts
(obtained by simulating the noisy circuit under the model-output channel) and the
measured distribution. Because simulating the noisy circuit exactly is expensive, we use
circuits in a Clifford-dominated regime where efficient classical simulation of the
noisy dynamics is tractable, supplemented by a smaller set of near-Clifford circuits
evaluated with tensor-network methods. We regularise toward the baseline model so that,
in the low-data limit, the learned model degrades gracefully to the established
state-of-the-art rather than to noise.

### 4.5 Integration into mitigation

For PEC, the learned channel is inverted per layer to produce the quasi-probability
decomposition, exactly as in the baseline pipeline but with context-dependent rates. For
ZNE, we use the learned model to choose noise-amplification factors and to inform the
extrapolation functional form, replacing the usual assumption of a fixed polynomial. In
both cases the mitigation algorithm is unchanged; only the noise model feeding it is
swapped, which isolates the contribution of the model itself.

### 4.6 Sampling-cost accounting

PEC pays for unbiasedness with a sampling overhead that grows exponentially in the total
error rate of the circuit. A noise model that is more accurate but implies a larger
quasi-probability norm could, in principle, raise that overhead even as it lowers bias.
Any honest comparison must therefore hold the shot budget fixed and report bias at equal
cost, not bias alone. We define the comparison precisely: for each benchmark circuit we
allocate an identical total number of shots to the baseline pipeline and to the learned
pipeline, distribute those shots according to each method's own sampling distribution, and
compare the resulting bias and variance of the mitigated estimator. If the learned model
lowers bias only by spending more shots, that is not an improvement, and our accounting
will surface it rather than hide it. We will also report the sampling overhead itself as a
function of depth, since a model that improves accuracy but blows up the overhead is of
limited practical use.

### 4.7 Avoiding leakage between training and evaluation

A subtle failure mode is data leakage: if the circuits, qubit subsets, or calibration
epochs used to train the model overlap with those used to evaluate it, the reported
advantage is inflated. We enforce three separations. First, circuit-structure separation:
the evaluation circuits come from a circuit family disjoint from the training family.
Second, spatial separation: a subset of qubit pairs is held out entirely from training so
that crosstalk generalisation can be tested on unseen geometry. Third, temporal
separation: evaluation uses calibration epochs that postdate the training window, which
tests whether the model truly conditions on current device state rather than memorising a
snapshot. Only results that survive all three separations count toward the headline claim.

## 5. Evaluation plan

We evaluate at three levels.

**Model level (RQ1, RQ2).** On a held-out set of tomographically characterised gate
sequences and qubit subsets, we compare the learned model and the baseline by KL
divergence and by total-variation distance between predicted and measured distributions.
For RQ2 we ablate input features (removing neighbour-gate features, removing timestamps)
and check whether crosstalk and drift signatures vanish, which would confirm the model is
using that information rather than overfitting.

**Mitigation level (RQ3).** On benchmark circuits with classically computable ideal
expectation values (for example Trotterised transverse-field Ising dynamics in regimes
still simulable), we measure the bias of mitigated estimates under the learned model
versus the baseline, at matched shot budgets. The headline metric is the ratio of
absolute biases. We pre-register a target of at least a two-fold bias reduction at depth
40 and will report the result whether or not it is met.

**Scaling level (RQ4).** We sweep circuit depth and the number of active qubits and plot
bias and sampling overhead jointly, locating the crossover depth beyond which PEC's
overhead makes the learned model's advantage uneconomical.

Crucially, every comparison holds the mitigation algorithm and the shot budget fixed and
varies only the noise model. We will report negative and partial results, and we will
release the trained model, the circuit sets, and the analysis code so that others can
reproduce and contest the findings.

## 6. Risks and mitigations

**Risk: the learned model overfits to a particular calibration epoch.** Device drift
means a model trained this week may be stale next week. Mitigation: we include
timestamped calibration data as input so the model conditions on the current device
state rather than memorising one snapshot, and we test on data from epochs held out in
time, not just held out by circuit.

**Risk: classical simulability of the training circuits limits the regime we can train
in.** Our training objective needs a classically computable reference, which confines us
to Clifford-dominated and near-Clifford circuits. The learned model may not extrapolate
to deeply non-Clifford regimes. Mitigation: we characterise this limit explicitly,
quantify how performance degrades as circuits move away from the Clifford regime, and are
candid that the method inherits the simulability frontier as a hard boundary.

**Risk: the interpretability constraint costs accuracy.** By forcing the output into a
Pauli-Lindblad form we may leave structure uncaptured. Mitigation: we run an
unconstrained-model arm purely as a diagnostic upper bound on achievable fit, not for
deployment, so we know how much accuracy the constraint costs.

**Risk: the two-fold target is missed.** The pre-registered threshold may not be reached.
This is a scientific outcome, not a failure of execution, and the proposal is structured
so that a null result on RQ3 is still informative about the limits of model-based
mitigation.

## 7. Timeline

The project runs over 24 months.

- **Months 1 to 4.** Build the data-collection pipeline; establish the Pauli-Lindblad
  baseline on both platforms; reproduce published PEC results as a sanity check.
- **Months 5 to 10.** Develop and train the graph-network noise model; complete RQ1 and
  RQ2 evaluations at the model level.
- **Months 11 to 16.** Integrate the learned model into PEC and ZNE; run RQ3 mitigation
  comparisons on the superconducting device.
- **Months 17 to 20.** Scaling study (RQ4); replication on the trapped-ion platform.
- **Months 21 to 24.** Analysis, ablations, write-up, and public release of code, models,
  and datasets.

Milestones gate the schedule: if RQ1 fails at month 10, we pivot to diagnosing why the
learned model cannot beat the baseline, which is itself a publishable contribution.

this literature is to compare a freshly tuned learned model against a baseline that was
never given the same engineering care, which inflates the apparent advantage. By spending
the first four months reproducing published PEC results to within their stated error bars,
we earn the right to claim that any later improvement is real rather than an artefact of an
under-tuned comparison. We budget a full month of slack across the project for hardware
queue delays and recalibration windows, which are unavoidable on shared cloud devices.

rather than compromise the Clifford-dominated core.

## 8. Reproducibility and open science

Mitigation results in this area have occasionally proven hard to reproduce because the
exact circuit families, calibration snapshots, and shot allocations were not published
alongside the headline numbers. We commit to releasing four artefacts: the raw
randomised-circuit measurement dataset with calibration metadata and timestamps, the
trained graph-network model weights, the full mitigation and analysis pipeline as code,
and a manifest mapping every figure in the eventual papers to the exact data and seed that
produced it. We will also publish the negative controls, the unconstrained-model
diagnostic arm and any research question where the learned model fails to beat the
baseline, so that the record is not skewed by selective reporting. Reviewers and
competitors should be able to take the released materials and either reproduce our central
comparison or demonstrate where it breaks.

A second reproducibility concern is device drift: a result obtained on one calibration
epoch may not hold weeks later when the hardware has been recalibrated. We address this by
reporting every mitigation comparison across at least three distinct calibration epochs
and presenting the spread, not a single best run. A claim that survives across epochs is
far more credible than one tuned to a lucky day on the machine.

## 9. Broader significance

If the central hypothesis holds, the immediate consequence is practical: existing PEC and
ZNE deployments could improve their accuracy at no extra sampling cost simply by swapping
in a better-informed noise model, since the mitigation algorithms themselves are
unchanged. The longer-term significance is methodological. It would establish that the
residual structure left behind by physics-based noise models, crosstalk, drift, and weak
non-Markovian memory, is both real and learnable, and that capturing it pays off
downstream. That would reframe noise characterisation as a learning problem with a clear
objective rather than a one-off calibration exercise.

If the hypothesis fails, the contribution is still substantive. A clean negative result,
that a flexible learned model trained on rich calibration context cannot beat a sparse
Pauli-Lindblad baseline inside PEC, would tell the field that the baseline already
captures the mitigation-relevant structure and that effort is better spent elsewhere, for
example on reducing the sampling overhead of PEC rather than on refining the noise model.
Either way the controlled design converts the question into evidence.

## 10. Expected contributions

The project will deliver (i) an open dataset of randomised-circuit measurements with rich
calibration context across two hardware platforms, (ii) a context-dependent,
physically constrained learned noise model with an audited account of what structure it
captures, (iii) a controlled measurement of how much such a model improves PEC and ZNE
at fixed cost, and (iv) an honest map of the regimes where the approach helps and where
its overhead or simulability constraints make it uneconomical. Whether the headline
hypothesis holds or not, the controlled design ensures the result advances understanding
of model-limited error mitigation on NISQ hardware.

Mitigation results in this area have occasionally proven hard to reproduce because the
exact circuit families, calibration snapshots, and shot allocations were not published
alongside the headline numbers. We commit to releasing four artefacts: the raw

trained graph-network model weights, the full mitigation and analysis pipeline as code,

produced it. We will also publish the negative controls, the unconstrained-model
diagnostic arm and any research question where the learned model fails to beat the
baseline, so that the record is not skewed by selective reporting. Reviewers and

comparison or demonstrate where it breaks.

If the central hypothesis holds, the immediate consequence is practical: existing PEC and

unchanged. The longer-term significance is methodological. It would establish that the

Pauli-Lindblad baseline inside PEC, would tell the field that the baseline already

calibration context across two hardware platforms, (ii) a context-dependent,
physically constrained learned noise model with an audited account of what structure it

to Clifford-dominated and near-Clifford circuits. The learned model may not extrapolate

quantify how performance degrades as circuits move away from the Clifford regime, and are

Pauli-Lindblad form we may leave structure uncaptured. Mitigation: we run an
unconstrained-model arm purely as a diagnostic upper bound on achievable fit, not for
deployment, so we know how much accuracy the constraint costs.

This is a scientific outcome, not a failure of execution, and the proposal is structured
so that a null result on RQ3 is still informative about the limits of model-based
mitigation.

## 7. Timeline

The project runs over 24 months.

- **Months 1 to 4.** Build the data-collection pipeline; establish the Pauli-Lindblad
  baseline on both platforms; reproduce published PEC results as a sanity check.
- **Months 5 to 10.** Develop and train the graph-network noise model; complete RQ1 and

- **Months 11 to 16.** Integrate the learned model into PEC and ZNE; run RQ3 mitigation
  comparisons on the superconducting device.
- **Months 17 to 20.** Scaling study (RQ4); replication on the trapped-ion platform.
- **Months 21 to 24.** Analysis, ablations, write-up, and public release of code, models,
  and datasets.

learned model cannot beat the baseline, which is itself a publishable contribution.

this literature is to compare a freshly tuned learned model against a baseline that was
never given the same engineering care, which inflates the apparent advantage. By spending
the first four months reproducing published PEC results to within their stated error bars,
we earn the right to claim that any later improvement is real rather than an artefact of an
under-tuned comparison. We budget a full month of slack across the project for hardware
queue delays and recalibration windows, which are unavoidable on shared cloud devices.

The project requires one postdoctoral researcher with experience in open quantum-system
simulation, one doctoral student focused on the machine-learning architecture, and shared
access to classical compute for tensor-network simulation of the near-Clifford reference
circuits. Cloud access to both hardware platforms is budgeted at a level sufficient for
the randomised-circuit data collection described in Section 4.2, with the trapped-ion
replication scoped as a smaller campaign than the superconducting work because its role is
confirmatory rather than primary. We note one resource risk explicitly: tensor-network

exact circuit families, calibration snapshots, and shot allocations were not published

diagnostic arm and any research question where the learned model fails to beat the
baseline, so that the record is not skewed by selective reporting. Reviewers and
competitors should be able to take the released materials and either reproduce our central
comparison or demonstrate where it breaks.

and presenting the spread, not a single best run. A claim that survives across epochs is
far more credible than one tuned to a lucky day on the machine.

If the central hypothesis holds, the immediate consequence is practical: existing PEC and
ZNE deployments could improve their accuracy at no extra sampling cost simply by swapping

unchanged. The longer-term significance is methodological. It would establish that the

calibration context across two hardware platforms, (ii) a context-dependent,
physically constrained learned noise model with an audited account of what structure it
captures, (iii) a controlled measurement of how much such a model improves PEC and ZNE

of model-limited error mitigation on NISQ hardware.

# How mRNA Vaccines Teach the Body to Fight Disease

For most of the twentieth century, making a vaccine meant working with the pathogen itself. Scientists grew a virus, weakened or killed it, and injected the result so the immune system could learn to recognise the real thing. This approach saved countless lives, but it was slow, and it carried the awkward requirement of handling large quantities of the very thing you wanted to protect people against. mRNA vaccines take a different route. Instead of delivering the pathogen, they deliver a set of instructions and let the body build a harmless piece of the pathogen on its own.

## The recipe analogy

Think of your cells as kitchens. A kitchen does not store finished meals from every restaurant in town; it stores recipes and cooks on demand. DNA is the master cookbook, kept safely in the nucleus. When a cell needs a particular protein, it copies the relevant page into a short, disposable note called messenger RNA, or mRNA. That note travels out to the kitchen counter, the ribosome, where the protein is assembled ingredient by ingredient. Once the job is done, the note is thrown away.

An mRNA vaccine is, in effect, a recipe card slipped into the kitchen from outside. It does not rewrite the master cookbook. It simply asks the cell to cook one specific dish: a single, recognisable protein from the target pathogen. For the vaccines against the virus that causes COVID-19, that dish is the spike protein, the knob-like structure the virus uses to latch onto human cells.

## What happens after the injection

The mRNA on its own is fragile and would be chewed up almost immediately in the bloodstream. So vaccine designers wrap it in a tiny bubble of fat called a lipid nanoparticle. This bubble protects the message and helps it slip inside cells near the injection site, mostly muscle cells and certain immune cells. Once inside, the cell reads the instructions and produces copies of the spike protein. Crucially, it produces only the spike, never the whole virus. There is no way for the vaccine to assemble a working, infectious pathogen, because the recipe for the rest of the virus is simply not there.

The newly made spike proteins are then displayed on the surface of the cell or released into the surrounding tissue. To the immune system, this looks suspicious. Patrolling immune cells notice the unfamiliar protein and raise the alarm. Two main defences swing into action. B cells learn to produce antibodies, small proteins that stick to the spike and block it. T cells learn to recognise and destroy any cell that is displaying the spike, which in a real infection would mean cells that the virus has hijacked.

## Why the memory matters

The point of all this is not the immediate response but the lasting one. After the threat is dealt with, most of the activated immune cells die off, but a small reserve of memory cells remains. These cells are the immune system's filed notes. If the real virus ever appears, the memory cells recognise the spike immediately and mount a fast, strong response, often before the person feels ill at all. This is the same principle behind every vaccine. What is new is only the delivery method.

## How the message disappears

A common worry is that the injected instructions might linger or somehow reach the DNA in the nucleus. They do not. mRNA is inherently short-lived; the cell breaks it down within hours to a few days using the same machinery it uses for its own messenger RNA. And mRNA cannot be written back into DNA in human cells under normal conditions, because the cell lacks the specialised tools that would be required and the mRNA never enters the nucleus in the first place. Once the message is gone, the cell stops making the spike protein. What remains is the learning, held in the memory cells, not in any leftover vaccine.

## Speed and flexibility

The most striking practical advantage of the mRNA approach is speed. Because the manufacturing process is largely the same regardless of which protein you encode, updating a vaccine can be as simple as swapping in a new recipe. Designers change the sequence of the message, keep the lipid wrapping and the production line the same, and test the result. This is why mRNA vaccines could be developed against a brand-new virus in months rather than years, and why the platform is now being explored for other diseases, from influenza to certain cancers.

## A balanced picture

None of this makes mRNA vaccines magical. They must be kept cold, which complicates distribution in places without reliable refrigeration. Like all vaccines they can cause side effects, usually mild and short-lived, such as a sore arm or a day of feeling run down as the immune system does its work. And the technology is newer in widespread use than older vaccine types, so long-term monitoring continues, as it should for any medical product. These are real considerations, not reasons for alarm.

The core idea, though, is elegant in its simplicity. Rather than showing the body a weakened enemy, an mRNA vaccine hands over a single, safe blueprint and trusts the body's own kitchens to do the cooking and its own memory to keep the lesson. The pathogen never has to enter the room.

# Social Media Is the Single Cause of Everything Wrong With Young People Today

Walk into any room of teenagers and you will see the same thing: heads bowed, thumbs scrolling, eyes glazed. There is no longer any mystery about what has gone wrong with the young. It is the phones, and more precisely it is social media. Every problem we see in young people today, anxiety, loneliness, poor grades, bad posture, shrinking attention spans, political extremism, eating disorders, and a general inability to cope with life, traces back to one source and one source only. Remove social media and you remove the rot.

Consider the evidence of your own eyes. A generation ago, children played outside. They climbed trees, built dens, argued in person, and came home filthy and happy. Today they sit indoors staring at screens. The contrast could not be starker, and the conclusion could not be plainer. The screens did this. Nothing else has changed.

The anxiety epidemic is the clearest proof. Rates of anxiety among teenagers have climbed steadily, and over the same period social media use has exploded. The two lines on the graph rise together. When two things rise together like that, only a fool would deny that one causes the other. The platforms are engineered to be addictive, after all, and an addicted mind is an anxious mind. Case closed.

Then there is the matter of attention. Teachers everywhere complain that students cannot focus, cannot read a long book, cannot sit through a lesson. Of course they cannot. They have spent their whole lives being fed three-second videos, each one more stimulating than the last. The brain rewires itself around this constant drip of novelty, and once rewired it cannot be put back. An entire generation has had its capacity for deep thought destroyed before it ever developed.

Loneliness follows the same pattern. We are told that young people have hundreds of online friends, yet they have never been lonelier. The reason is obvious. A like is not a hug. A comment is not a conversation. By replacing real human contact with hollow digital substitutes, social media has left a generation starving in the middle of a feast. They are connected to everyone and close to no one.

Look too at the comparison that never stops running. On these platforms every young person measures their ordinary life against the curated highlights of everyone they have ever met, and a few thousand strangers besides. The holidays they did not take, the bodies they do not have, the parties they were not invited to, all of it scrolls past in an endless ribbon of other people winning. No mind, least of all a developing one, was built to absorb that volume of comparison. It is no wonder self-esteem has collapsed. The platforms have turned adolescence, already a fragile time, into a permanent and unwinnable contest, and they have done it on purpose, because envy keeps people scrolling and scrolling is what they sell.

And consider sleep, the quiet casualty in all of this. The phone goes to bed with them, glowing on the pillow, buzzing through the night with notifications engineered to be impossible to ignore. A generation that does not sleep is a generation that cannot learn, cannot regulate its moods, cannot grow. Every one of the troubles already listed is made worse by exhaustion, and the exhaustion comes from the same glowing rectangle. Strip it away and the body would do what bodies have always done: rest, and repair, and wake up well. The platforms have stolen even that.

Some will object that other factors might be at work. They will point to economic pressures, to the cost of housing, to academic competition, to climate dread, to the lingering effects of a pandemic that shut schools for months, to changes in parenting, to the decline of community institutions. This is exactly the kind of hand-wringing that lets the real culprit off the hook. These so-called factors are distractions. If they mattered, young people in every era would have suffered equally, and they did not. The one new thing in the lives of the young is the smartphone in their pocket. Everything else is noise.

The defenders of these platforms will also say that social media has benefits. They will mention that isolated teenagers find community online, that marginalised young people find others like them, that activists organise, that friendships stretched across distance are kept alive. Even if such things occasionally happen, they cannot begin to outweigh the wholesale destruction of a generation's mental health. You do not praise a poison for its pleasant aftertaste.

What, then, is to be done? The answer is as simple as the diagnosis. Ban social media for anyone under eighteen. Not restrict it, not regulate it, not teach children to use it wisely. Ban it outright. Half-measures will fail because the platforms are too clever and too addictive to be tamed. Only total removal will work. Parents who hesitate are failing their children. Politicians who hesitate are failing the nation.

We did not always tolerate things that poisoned the young. We took lead out of petrol. We put cigarettes behind the counter. We demanded seatbelts. In every case there were those who said the problem was complicated, that many factors were involved, that we should be cautious. They were wrong then and their descendants are wrong now. Some problems really do have a single cause and a single cure. This is one of them.

The young are not broken by nature. They have been broken by a product, deliberately engineered to hook them, sold to them by companies that knew exactly what they were doing. The evidence is in front of us, written on every bowed head and every anxious face. We can keep pretending it is complicated, or we can act. There is nothing else to discuss.

# Tracking Climate-Driven Range Shifts Through Citizen-Science Birdsong

## Motivation

As the climate warms, many bird species are shifting where they live, generally towards the poles and to higher elevations, tracking the conditions they are adapted to. Documenting these shifts at fine spatial and temporal resolution is hard. Traditional bird surveys depend on skilled observers in the field, are expensive to run at scale, and tend to be sparse in exactly the remote areas where range edges are moving. Meanwhile, members of the public now record enormous quantities of birdsong on their phones and through apps such as those that identify species from audio. This proposal asks whether that growing archive of citizen-science audio can be turned into a reliable instrument for measuring climate-driven range shifts.

## Core idea

Birdsong is a strong proxy for presence. A species that is singing in a place is, by definition, present there during the breeding season, when most song occurs. If we can reliably identify species from crowd-sourced recordings and attach trustworthy time and location stamps to them, then the leading edge of a species' range becomes something we can watch move from one year to the next. The central hypothesis is that the poleward and upslope boundaries of a set of focal species will show measurable annual movement that correlates with local temperature anomalies, and that citizen-science audio can detect this movement at least as early as conventional surveys.

## Data

The primary data source is the audio already being uploaded by the public, together with the metadata each recording carries: a timestamp, an approximate GPS location, and in many cases an app-generated species label. We would partner with one or more existing platforms to obtain a de-identified feed of recordings and metadata, restricted to a defined study region, for example a north-south transect across a continent where range shifts are expected to be detectable. Temperature and other climate variables would come from standard gridded climate datasets.

## Method

The work has three stages. First, validation of the species labels. App-generated identifications are good but imperfect, and error rates vary by species and recording quality. We would draw a stratified sample of recordings and have expert ornithologists confirm or correct the labels, producing a per-species estimate of precision and recall. Species whose labels cannot be validated to an agreed threshold would be dropped from the analysis. This step is essential and is where many audio-based studies are weakest.

Second, range-edge estimation. For each focal species and each year, we would map the confirmed detections and estimate the position of the range boundary using an established quantile-based method, for instance the latitude or elevation below which a fixed high percentage of detections fall. We would then test whether that boundary moves across years and whether its movement tracks temperature anomalies.

Third, bias correction. Citizen-science data are not collected uniformly. People record more near cities, near roads, at weekends, and during good weather. If we ignore this, an apparent range shift might be nothing more than a shift in where people happen to be recording. We would model recording effort explicitly, using the total volume of recordings of all species in a cell as a measure of observer effort, and correct detections accordingly. We would also run a placebo test on resident, non-shifting species: if our pipeline reports them moving, the bias correction has failed.

## Feasibility

The pieces of this project already exist. The audio is being collected now, in volumes that dwarf any professional survey. Automated identification is mature enough to give a starting label. The statistical tools for range-edge estimation and for modelling spatial sampling bias are established in the ecological literature. The novelty is in combining them and in treating the validation and bias-correction steps as first-class parts of the method rather than afterthoughts. A two-year pilot on five to ten well-recorded species in a single region would be enough to show whether the approach detects known shifts and survives the placebo test.

## Expected outcomes and limitations

If it works, the payoff is an early-warning system for range shifts that is cheap, continuous, and densest in populated areas, complementing rather than replacing expert surveys. If it does not work, the project will still produce a quantified account of how far citizen-science audio can be trusted for this purpose, which is itself useful.

The limitations are real and we name them plainly. The method only sees species that sing and only during the singing season, so it is blind to non-vocal birds and to silent parts of the year. It depends on the continued goodwill and activity of volunteers, whose behaviour may change. The location stamps are only as accurate as the phones that produced them. And presence-only data tell us where a species is, not where it is absent, which complicates any claim that a species has retreated from somewhere. The placebo test and the effort model are designed to contain these problems, not to eliminate them.

## Why it matters

Range shifts are among the clearest fingerprints of climate change on living systems, and the species moving fastest are often those at the edges of their ranges, where professional monitoring is thinnest. A method that turns the public's own recordings into a dense, continuous signal of where birds are singing, with its uncertainties measured rather than hidden, would put a useful new instrument in the hands of ecologists at very low marginal cost.

Tomas had died three years ago in a car crash on the coast road. The plan was simple. Go back, warn him, change the day. Mara had checked the calculations a hundred times. She stepped into the chamber, set the dial for a morning three years gone, and pulled the lever.

The world folded like wet paper. When it unfolded she was standing in the same lab, but the calendar on the wall read three years earlier, and the light through the high window was the particular thin gold of an autumn morning. It was beautiful, she thought, the way old light always looked slightly used, as if it had passed through too many afternoons to be entirely new.

She drove to Tomas's flat. He answered the door in his dressing gown, holding a mug, alive and irritated.

'Mara? It's seven in the morning.'

'You can't drive the coast road today,' she said. 'Promise me. Please.'

He laughed at her. He always laughed. But she could see in his face that he believed her, because she was crying, and Tomas had never been able to bear her crying. He promised. She drove home happy for the first time in three years.

When she got back to the lab, everything was the same. The calendar still read three years earlier. She waited. She made tea. She read a book she had already read. After a while she realised she did not know how to get home, because she had only ever planned the journey out. This did not worry her as much as it should have.

She spent the first night on the floor of the lab, under a coat, listening to the coils tick as they cooled. Outside, the city went about its business three years too soon. Buses she remembered scrapping still ran. A shop she had watched close was open and lit. It was, she thought, like walking through a photograph of her own life, everything in its place and nothing quite able to see her. She found she did not mind. Tomas was alive somewhere across the river, drinking tea in his dressing gown, and that single fact made the strangeness bearable, even sweet.

In the morning she tried to think clearly about the machine. The chamber was here, the coils were here, but the version of her that knew how to send it forward was three years away, in a future that, if everything had worked, no longer contained a dead brother and so might not contain the grieving woman who had built the thing at all. The logic of it slid out of her hands whenever she reached for it. She made more tea instead. The kettle, at least, behaved the way kettles always had.

Days passed. Then a strange thing happened. A second Mara walked into the lab, the Mara of three years ago, the one who had not yet lost her brother and did not yet know how to build a time machine. The two Maras looked at each other. The younger one did not seem surprised at all.

'I've been expecting you,' the younger Mara said, which was odd, because there was no reason she should have been.

They talked for a long time. The older Mara explained everything, the crash, the grief, the machine. The younger Mara nodded along as if it were a recipe for soup. Then she asked the obvious question.

'If you saved Tomas, why do you still remember him dying?'

The older Mara did not have an answer. She had not thought about it. She decided it did not matter, and the younger Mara agreed, and they had lunch.

That afternoon the phone rang. It was Tomas. He was calling from the coast road. He had decided to drive it after all, just to prove he was not afraid, because that was the kind of man he was, although he had never once been that kind of man in any of Mara's memories. There was a sound on the line like the sea swallowing something. Then nothing.

Both Maras sat in the lab in the thin gold light. The older one felt the grief arrive again, familiar as a coat. The younger one, who had not known Tomas was going to die until this exact moment, somehow grieved in perfect step with her, as if she had always known.

'We could try again,' the younger Mara said.

'We could always try again,' said the older.

When it unfolded she was standing in the same lab, and the calendar on the wall read three years earlier, and the light through the high window was the particular thin gold of an autumn morning. 'Nothing,' she said. 'I just wanted to see you.'

He softened. He let her in. They drank tea together in the autumn light, and for one morning nobody warned anybody about anything, and the sea stayed where it was, far away and patient, and the machine waited in the lab for whatever she decided to do next, which even she did not yet know.
